feedback: If the child grabs 4 counters for 1/4, share the 12 into 4 equal groups on the tray; one group (3 counters) is 1/4 — the 4 counts the GROUPS, not the objects.
If the child gives 3 for 3/4, ask how many of the four groups 3/4 wants — three of them — and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
When the set changes from 12 counters to 8 and is re-shared, point out each ring now holds 2: the same fraction 1/4 gives a different amount because the whole set has changed.
activities.intendedInsight: The whole is the whole SET; the denominator counts the equal groups to make and the numerator counts the groups to take. The same fraction names a different quantity when the set changes, so a fraction is a relationship, not a fixed number of objects.
learnerActions: Start with 12 counters and the request 'show me 1/4'. Set the denominator to 4 and form four group-rings (or draw four rings/circles on paper).
Deal the 12 counters out one at a time so each ring holds an equal share — 3 each. If any group is unequal, keep dealing until they match.
Take one group for 1/4: say and record '1/4 of 12 = 3'.
For 3/4, light up / shade / move three of the four groups and count 3 + 3 + 3 = 9; record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Change the set size: re-share 8 counters into four equal groups and see each group is now 2, so 1/4 of 8 = 2. Compare with 1/4 of 12 = 3.
State in words why 1/4 means making 4 equal groups rather than just taking 4 counters.
activities.title: Share the set into equal groups, then take some

feedback: If the child writes 3/9, point out they compared coloured to uncoloured; count the coloured against the WHOLE set (all 12): 3 out of 12 = 3/12. The denominator is the whole, not the leftover.
Reinforce reading the name aloud ('three twelfths') to avoid treating the digits as a count.
activities.intendedInsight: Naming a fraction of a set is part-to-whole: compare the coloured objects to the whole set, not to the uncoloured remainder.
learnerActions: Look at a set of 12 counters with 3 coloured. Decide what fraction is coloured.
Count the coloured objects (3) and then count the WHOLE set (all 12), not the uncoloured ones.
Explain why it is 3/12 and not 3/9: the denominator is the whole set, not the leftover uncoloured counters.
Say the fraction by name ('three twelfths') rather than 'three over twelve'.
activities.title: Name the coloured fraction of a set — part to whole
